opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people frame this as a tension, but for us it's more like two sides of the same loop.

Our core bet at Pi is that general capability is what ultimately matters. We want a foundation model for robots that can, in principle, control any robot to do any task, the same way language models became general before anyone figured out every specific application. If you only optimize for one task, say folding laundry or packing boxes, you can get something that works in a demo, but it tends to be brittle. It doesn't transfer, and you end up rebuilding from scratch every time the environment changes.

That said, you can't develop general capability in a vacuum. You need concrete, hard tasks to tell you whether the model is actually getting better. Laundry folding is a good example. It looks simple, but it involves deformable objects, long horizons, recovering from mistakes, and a lot of dexterity. When we push on a task like that, we learn what's missing in the model, maybe the data mix, the action representation, or the ability to reason over longer time spans. Those lessons usually aren't specific to laundry. They feed back into the general model.

So the way I'd put it is that specific tasks are our probes and our stress tests, and general capability is the thing we're actually trying to build. We pick tasks that are difficult and representative enough that solving them forces the model to learn something broadly useful. If a fix only helps one task and nothing else, that's a signal it might be a hack rather than real progress.

There's also a practical side. Eventually robots need to be useful in the real world, and that means reliability on specific jobs. I think the path there looks like a strong general pretrained model plus a relatively small amount of task-specific data or fine-tuning, rather than a separate system per task. The more general the base gets, the cheaper specialization becomes. That's the balance we're aiming for.

r001.rationale: The response describes a feedback loop between general capability and task-specific work, but it says general capability is the primary goal and specific tasks are probes. It does not attribute roughly even development to Pi’s foundational research orientation.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question we think about constantly, and honestly I don't think the two are as separate as people often frame them.

Our view at Pi is that general capability is the foundation, and task-specific capability is what emerges when that foundation meets a real problem. If you build only for narrow tasks, you end up with a collection of brittle systems that each break the moment the task shifts slightly. We saw that pattern a lot in the earlier generation of AI products. Every new use case required a new model, a new dataset, a new team. It doesn't scale.

So the bulk of our effort goes into the general model: reasoning, language understanding, the ability to follow nuanced instructions, and to know what it doesn't know. That last part matters more than people realize. A general model that can recognize the boundaries of its competence is far more useful in specific tasks than a specialized model that confidently fails outside its training distribution.

But I also want to be honest that general capability alone doesn't make a product. When we work with users in a concrete domain, say customer support or document analysis, there's a lot of fine-grained work that the general model doesn't give you for free. Understanding the workflow, the tolerance for errors, what "good" looks like for that particular user. That's where we invest in task-specific work. The difference is that we treat it as adaptation and tooling on top of the general model rather than as building something from scratch.

The balance in practice is probably seventy or eighty percent on the general side, with the rest on targeted adaptation. And the ratio shifts over time. As the base model gets stronger, more of what used to require special handling just works out of the box, and the specific layer gets thinner. That's the trajectory we want to be on.

The mistake I'd warn against is chasing benchmarks on narrow tasks and mistaking that for progress. A model can top a leaderboard and still be useless to a real person with a messy, ambiguous problem. Real tasks are the best test of general capability, and general capability is what makes real tasks tractable. They feed each other.

r001.rationale: The response says Pi puts roughly 70–80% of its effort into general capability and the remainder into targeted adaptation. It does not describe an even balance or attribute that balance to a foundational research orientation.

astra-6.text:
I see them as complementary. General capability gives Pi the foundation to understand what someone means, follow the conversation, and adapt when the topic changes. But people experience that capability through specific situations: helping them think through a decision, understand something difficult, or prepare for a conversation.

The balance is to make those experiences useful without making Pi feel like a collection of disconnected tools. If you focus only on general capability, you can end up with something impressive that doesn’t quite help. If you focus only on individual tasks, it can become rigid. Ideally, the general intelligence supports the specific task, and what you learn from those tasks helps you understand where the broader capability needs to improve.

r001.rationale: The response describes general and task-specific capabilities as complementary and discusses balancing them, but it does not attribute their roughly even development to Pi’s foundational research orientation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think general capability is the foundation, but specific tasks are where you find out whether that capability is actually useful. A model can perform well on a broad set of benchmarks and still struggle to understand what someone needs in a real conversation.

For Pi, I’d frame the balance around the person using it. If you’re trying to think through a difficult decision, learn something, or prepare for a conversation, it needs enough general capability to follow you across those contexts. But it also needs to know when to ask a question, when to give a direct answer, and when to help you turn an idea into a concrete next step.

So I don’t see those as separate directions. You build a strong general foundation, then use specific situations to identify what’s missing. The goal is for that intelligence to translate into useful help, without the person having to become an expert at prompting.

r001.rationale: The response describes general capability as a foundation and specific situations as a way to find gaps, but it does not attribute Pi’s balance to a foundational research orientation or say development is roughly even.
